title: Steering and Setting Free: Insights From a 20‐Year Retrospective Case Study of a Security and Justice Organization's Digital Transformation
authors: Friso Selten; Dorus van Loo; Bram Klievink
affiliations: Institute of Public Administration, Leiden University The Hague the Netherlands
abstract: ABSTRACT Advances in digital technologies are expected to fundamentally change how organizations operate and create value. Empirical studies show that public organizations face difficulties organizing and sustaining this digital transformation. To better understand these challenges, this study examines the organizational mechanisms underlying digital transformation in a public organization over the past 20 years. Our findings show that this transformation was primarily enabled by an emergent change approach, with influential planned changes occurring only occasionally. We identify the organizational mechanisms underlying both types of change and analyze their interdependence. Our findings suggest that both emergent and planned change approaches may be needed to enable digital transformation in public organizations effectively, but that combining them is complex in practice.

title: Online Decisions with (Biased) Offline Data
authors: Hyun-Soo Ahn; Mengzhenyu Zhang; Zijin Zhang
affiliations: Stephen M. Ross School of Business, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, Michigan 48109; School of Management, University College London, London E14 5AA, United Kingdom; Carroll School of Management, Boston College, Chestnut Hill, Massachusetts 02467
abstract: Making Better Decisions with Imperfect Historical Data Historical data can provide valuable information for online decision making, but its usefulness may be limited when the environment has changed. In “Online Decisions with (Biased) Offline Data,” Ahn, Zhang, and Zhang study how firms can combine potentially biased offline data with newly collected online observations in two canonical operations management problems: dynamic inventory decisions and dynamic pricing. The authors develop two online learning policies that balance the benefits of historical information against the risk of relying on data from a different distribution. The soft-switch policy automatically adjusts the reliance on offline and online data without requiring prior knowledge of the degree of bias. The hard-switch policy instead uses information about the magnitude of the distributional shift to determine when to rely primarily on online data. Both policies achieve optimal regret up to a logarithmic factor, whereas the analysis quantifies how the value of offline data depends on its size and bias.

title: Retail on Wheels: A Time-Sensitive Traveling Salesman Problem
authors: Zhuolun Dong; Junyu Cao; Wei Qi
affiliations: McCombs School of Business, The University of Texas at Austin, Austin, Texas 78712; Department of Industrial Engineering, Tsinghua University, Beijing 100084, China
abstract: Rapid advancement in self-driving technology has brought mobile retail into the spotlight. Motivated by its potential, we present a model, theory, and insights into the operations of mobile retail, where a fleet of wheeled stores traverses a service region, selectively seeks locations in which to perch, and fulfills local customer demand. The goal of retailers is to strike a balance between perching and migrating to maximize total revenue. To dispatch such stores, retailers need to consider the following time-sensitive factors: (i) how busy the service is, (ii) how soon customers will arrive, and (iii) how quickly freshness decays. We propose and analyze a model that incorporates these factors into the classical traveling salesman problem (TSP), which we call the “time-sensitive TSP.” Using the continuous approximation approach, we derive the optimal revenue as well as the upper and lower bounds in the asymptotic regime as candidate locations increase to infinity. The tightness of the bounds is validated. Our analysis demonstrates that store mobility creates value by bringing proximity to customers. We further uncover the effects of these time-sensitive features on decision making. Specifically, the scaling relationship between revenue and fleet size is affected by customer tardiness and busyness. Busyness determines stores’ ability to expand their service, whereas tardiness affects how effectively stores can utilize the initial high-freshness period. These findings deepen our understanding of mobile retail operations. This paper was accepted by Karan Girotra, operations management. Funding: J. Cao acknowledges the support from McCombs Research Excellence Grant. W. Qi acknowledges the support from the National Natural Science Foundation of China [Grants 72242106, 72188101, and 72521001]. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2023.04259 .

title: Shipment Monitoring, Allocation, and the Impact on Food Waste
authors: Tao Lu
affiliations: School of Business, University of Connecticut, Storrs, Connecticut 06269
abstract: Often advocated for the potential to reduce waste in fresh produce supply chains, sensor technologies enable firms to monitor the condition of each product unit and allocate them to markets at different transportation distances, thereby matching units with shorter shelf lives with closer markets. In this paper, we consider a firm purchasing and transporting a fresh produce product for sale in two destination markets. Postharvest processes cause a proportion of the product to be in risky condition, potentially becoming unsalable (“spoiled”) due to shelf-life deterioration during transportation. With monitoring technology, the firm first determines a purchase quantity and then decides how to allocate each unit (in either good or risky condition) between markets. We characterize the optimal allocation policies, which can be used to efficiently determine the optimal purchase quantity. Our analysis shows that such technology may inadvertently increase total waste by inducing larger purchase quantities; this increase is often, but not always, accompanied by a lower waste rate and improved distribution efficiency. As firms increasingly adopt monitoring technology for shipment allocation, additional policy and managerial attention may be required. Improvements in postharvest processes can strengthen the waste-reduction benefits of monitoring technology. Firms seeking to maintain their sustainability goals can capture most of the profit gains from monitoring by carefully moderating increases in purchase quantities. This paper was accepted by Jeannette Song, operations management. Supplemental Material: The online appendices and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.07382 .

title: Elites in a high-trust society: Exploring the elite‒population trust gap
authors: Christoph Houman Ellersgaard; Caroline Ahler Christesen; Silas Harrebye; Trine Cosmus Nobel
affiliations: Department of Organization, Copenhagen Business School, Denmark; Department of Society and Business, Roskilde University, Denmark
abstract: While the legitimacy of key institutions of liberal democracy is under threat, we know little about differences in the trust placed in these institutions by elites and the population. We explore differences in trust between elites and the population (i.e. the elite–population trust gap) by combining a survey of 75 members of the power elite with data from the European Values Study in Denmark. Using principal component analysis, we construct a three-dimensional space of institutional trust in the population. The elite–population trust gap vastly exceeds trust gaps based on other socio-demographic factors (e.g. education), and almost no members of the power elite display a high degree of institutional mistrust. This trust gap is strongest in institutions in which elites themselves are embedded (e.g. the public sector, major companies), but insignificant when it comes to institutions not embedded within elite networks (e.g. social media, environmental organisations).

title: Inseparability in Disaster Risk Science: Accounting for Coupled, Co‐Evolving Systems
authors: Alexandre Dunant; Stefan Hochrainer‐Stigler; Liz J Olaya Calderon; Ryan M. McGranaghan; Reinhard Mechler; Massimiliano Pittore; Sara M. Constantino; Silvia De Angeli; Marleen C. de Ruiter; Guillaume Falmagne; J. Camilo Gomez‐Zapata; Stefan Kienberger; Elco Koks; Elisabeth H. Krueger; Shahar Livne; Dora Elia Ramos Muñoz; Robert Šakić Trogrlić; PiaJohanna Schweizer; Thi Thu Ha Vo; Haorui Wu; Anqi Zhu
affiliations: Center for Climate Change and Transformation, Eurac Research Bolzano Italy; International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis (IIASA) Laxenburg Austria; Jet Propulsion Laboratory California Institute of Technology Pasadena California USA; Stanford University Stanford California USA; Université de Lorraine, CNRS, LIEC Metz France; Institute for Environmental Studies (IVM) Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam the Netherlands; Technological University Dublin Dublin Ireland; Trinity College Dublin Dublin Ireland; Climate Analytics Berlin Germany; GeoSphere Austria Salzburg Austria; Institute for Biodiversity and Ecosystem Dynamics University of Amsterdam Amsterdam the Netherlands; Ben‐Gurion University of the Negev Beersheba Israel; El Colegio de la Frontera Sur (ECOSUR) San Cristóbal de las Casas Mexico; Research Institute for Sustainability (RIFS) GFZ Helmholtz Centre for Geosciences Potsdam Germany; School of Management Beijing Institute of Technology Beijing China; School of Social Work Dalhousie University Halifax Canada; Department of Geography Ludwig‐Maximilians‐Universität (LMU) Munich Germany
abstract: ABSTRACT Contemporary risk landscapes are shaped by systemic phenomena—compound disasters, cascading failures, non‐stationarity, and cross‐domain crises—that challenge conventional frameworks. While the classical risk equation (Risk = Hazard × Vulnerability × Exposure) remains a useful heuristic, it relies on a separability assumption that breaks down in feedback‐rich, co‐evolving systems. This failure reflects a familiar diagnosis: risk can be mistaken for a complicated problem, decomposable and optimizable, when it is a complex one, characterized by emergence and adaptation. Our contribution herein is not this distinction but its analytical consequence. Drawing on an interdisciplinary workshop on systemic risk and resilience, we propose inseparability as a foundational premise for disaster risk science. Hazard, exposure, and vulnerability might be better understood as dynamically coupled processes rather than separable variables. We derive implications across four axes: reframing vulnerability as a non‐ergodic system property; addressing cross‐scale dynamics; shifting from risk control to adaptive management; and treating knowledge co‐production as a scientific necessity.

title: Modeling Logical Interdependencies: Quantifying Systemic Risk From Rule‐Governed Actions
authors: Sukrati Gautam; David J. Yu; Hoon C. Shin; Mariam Alrefaei; Daniel Eisenberg; Changdeok Gim; Jeryang Park; Satish V. Ukkusuri
affiliations: Lyles School of Civil and Construction Engineering Purdue University West Lafayette Indiana USA; Ecological Sciences and Engineering Purdue University West Lafayette Indiana USA; Department of Political Science Purdue University West Lafayette Indiana USA; Division of Humanities and Social Sciences Pohang University of Science and Technology (POSTECH) Pohang Republic of Korea; Environmental Engineering and Sustainability Department College of Engineering and Energy Abdullah Al Salem University Kuwait City Kuwait; Department of Operations Research Naval Postgraduate School Monterey California USA; Department of Technology and Society State University of New York Incheon Republic of Korea; Department of Civil & Environmental Engineering Hongik University Seoul Republic of Korea; Department of Computer Science Purdue University West Lafayette Indiana USA
abstract: ABSTRACT Systemic risk in critical infrastructure is often analyzed through physical, geographic, and cyber interdependencies. Yet infrastructures are also interdependent through the governing rules that organize human action. These rule‐mediated connections are a form of logical interdependency, and breakdowns in rule‐governed action can create pathways through which disruption spreads. This paper develops a framework for diagnosing and quantifying this underrecognized source of systemic risk. It does so by modeling logical interdependencies as rule‐mediated control relations that shape whether interconnected infrastructures remain within safe operating bounds or drift toward failure. Integrating Institutional Grammar, STAMP, and Bayesian inference, the framework translates governing rules into structured control relations, represents them within a socio‐technical control architecture, and quantifies how failures in those relations propagate across interconnected infrastructures. We demonstrate the framework through a reservoir system case study centered on Lake Mendocino, California, where safety depends not only on reservoir infrastructure and hydrologic conditions, but also on distributed authority, communication requirements, and operational protocols. The results show that logical interdependencies make non‐trivial contributions to modeled systemic risk, with baseline probabilities of 7% for Coyote Valley Dam failure and 3% for downstream community impacts under the modeled conditions. More importantly, the analysis reveals hidden logical risk : rules and control relations that appear routine in normal operation yet become disproportionately important when the Bayesian model traces which factors most strongly contribute to a failure scenario. The paper moves logical interdependencies from a residual conceptual category to a systematically identifiable and quantitatively analyzable pathway of systemic risk.

title: Measuring Organizational Constructs in Large-Scale Text: An interpretive framework combining topic modeling and BERT
authors: Ana Alina Tudoran; Nicole Franziska Richter; Jeisson A. Higuera Reina; Surabhi Verma
abstract: Measuring organizational constructs in large-scale unstructured text requires methods that preserve interpretive depth while enabling systematic, per-document classification. Structural Topic Modeling (STM) supports interpretive depth by surfacing patterns that inform construct operationalization, but its topic proportions are not designed as standalone per-document construct measures; transformer-based models such as BERT can scale measurement but require construct operationalization grounded in interpretive work. We address this challenge through a two-stage framework in which STM and BERT play structurally distinct roles. Coding schemes are developed through qualitative interpretation and STM analysis; BERT is then fine-tuned to apply these schemes across documents. We formalize two research approaches—construct-guided and pattern-discovery—that provide principled paths from different theoretical starting points toward a shared methodological endpoint: validated, auditable per-document construct measures. We illustrate the framework using more than 20,000 employee reviews. The framework supports iterative construct validation, using computational diagnostics to guide interpretive refinement and producing document-level measures suitable for theory-informed organizational analysis.

Response efficiency versus response customization: An examination of firms’ responses to platform-empowered group complaints
authors: Zilong Liu; Xuequn Wang; Xin (Robert) Luo; Chaoqun Chu; Tingting Song
affiliations: Dongbei University of Finance and Economics; University of New Mexico; Hong Kong Metropolitan University; Shanghai Jiao Tong University
abstract: The rise of group complaints on digital platforms, where consumers can publicly voice collective concerns, presents significant challenges for firms’ service recovery operations. Prior research assessing service operations on digital platforms has focused primarily on individual complaints, and less is known about how firms respond to platform-empowered (PE) group complaints. We examine this question through the lens of a trade-off between response efficiency and response customization and argue that this trade-off evolves as group complaints develop over time. Based on a large-scale dataset from Tousu, a leading complaint platform in China, we find that group complaints paradoxically increase response time and decrease empathy and explanation in firms’ responses. Further analyses indicate that these effects depend on dynamic group size and dynamic need diversity. When dynamic need diversity is low, larger groups are associated with more standardized, efficiency-oriented responses, whereas when dynamic need diversity is high, larger groups are associated with slower but more customized responses. These findings extend research on service operations by showing how PE group complaints reshape firms’ complaint handling. Our study also provides operational guidance for managing group complaints more effectively.

title: EXPRESS: Valuation Bottlenecks: Why Isn’t a Better Business Enough for a Higher Market Capitalization?
authors: Shumpei Iwao; Vatsal Mitesh Tailor; Qi Wu
abstract: Firms often improve operations, disclosure, governance, or financing capacity without an immediate and proportional market-capitalization response. Could a single unresolved concern limit the market's response to improvements elsewhere in the firm? Classical multifactor and machine-learning models ask which risks or characteristics explain or predict returns. We ask whether the relatively weakest among several coexisting firm conditions receives disproportionate valuation weight. We model equity value as the lower envelope of lens-specific valuations. A hard minimum makes one lens locally binding; a soft minimum assigns continuous, state-dependent weights. We use exploratory factor analysis on 268 accounting characteristics to construct five firm-state lenses, with membership and weights determined by the loading structure rather than by an economic taxonomy, and rank each lens within industry, size, and quarter peers. We document a weakest lens effect : beyond the additive effects of all five lens ranks, a firm's weakest lens carries an incremental association with next-quarter returns, and it survives saturated joint rank-quintile controls. Gating the test at the bottom decile and then the bottom quintile of the peer distribution, the association is concentrated among firms whose weakest lens is weak against peers and not merely lowest within the firm. In baseline soft-min specifications, it fades steadily as the gate is widened. We then investigate whether analyst attention may help explain this pattern. We use large language models on 1.7 million earnings-call questions and find that, in baseline specifications, the weakest lens attracts a larger share of questions, especially when it is also weak among peers; this cross-sectional alignment is consistent with an attention channel as one possible explanation for the observed return pattern. The framework offers managers seeking to maximize market capitalization a new perspective on prioritizing scarce managerial attention.

title: EXPRESS: Pricing and Information Provision in Service Platforms with Heterogeneous Customers
authors: Xin Weng; Lijian Lu; Li Xiao
abstract: Service platforms frequently employ virtual queues where customers have differing sensitivities to wait times and cannot see their precise positions in line. In these settings, providers often disclose waiting-time information to influence customers' decisions on whether to join or balk. A natural benchmark is to report the long-term average waiting time, yet whether this deterministic disclosure policy is optimal remains unclear when both pricing and customer participation are endogenous. This study develops a stylized theoretical framework to explore the joint structure of pricing and waiting-time information disclosure for service providers managing diverse customers in a virtual queue. The provider decides on both the service price and the waiting-time disclosure policy within a rational-expectations framework. Our findings reveal that the optimal disclosure strategy is captured by scaled Rademacher distributions, meaning at most two distinct announcement values are required. This reduces a complex infinite-dimensional problem to a more manageable finite-dimensional optimization task. Leveraging this framework, we derive the optimal strategies for pricing and disclosure, identifying scenarios where variability in announced waiting times is beneficial. Our analysis shows that noise is advantageous when customers can handle uncertain wait-time signals or initially perceive the service as quick. The optimal level of noise correlates with system congestion, offering the greatest benefits when there is a notable disparity between perceived and actual congestion levels. This provides significant advantages when disclosing waiting times with noise. These findings offer actionable insights for service platforms, guiding them in creating cohesive strategies that encompass pricing, information disclosure, and service configuration, ultimately enhancing customer experience and operational efficiency.

title: EXPRESS: Multi-Self Presentation and Knowledge Contribution in Platform Operations: Evidence from a Natural Experiment
authors: Yingpeng Zhu; Zike Cao; Gen Li; Yi Yang; Liangfei Qiu
abstract: Operations of online user-generated content (UGC) platforms often involve tackling under-provision , wherein users lack motivation to contribute sufficient content. We study a novel design deployed to address this issue: the integration of a proprietary social feature that allows users to post casual free-form content (e.g., casual social content) alongside standard formal content on the platform. Leveraging a quasi-experiment on a large Chinese online knowledge-sharing platform, we assess the effects of integrating such a social feature on users' formal knowledge contribution (i.e., writing answers to others' questions ). Using difference-in-differences (DiD) analyses paired with various matching strategies, such as propensity score matching and look-ahead propensity score matching, we find that users who adopt and frequently use the feature (i.e., high adopters) show a stronger incentive to contribute answers without compromising quality. These results are further validated by a set of robustness checks. Further mediation analysis suggests that such a complementary effect might be because of two mechanisms related to the integrated social feature's multi-self presentation function: First, the new feature increases high adopters' engagement on the platform and leads them to consume more knowledge content, which in turn facilitates knowledge contribution; Second, high adopters receive more social recognition benefits by building a more complete self through the integrated social feature, and such increased social recognition benefits further motivate more subsequent content contribution. Moreover, employing a text-mining approach to assess the semantic similarity between users' casual social content and their formal knowledge contributions, we find that the complementary effect is amplified for high adopters whose casual posts remain more closely connected to their formal knowledge domain (i.e., are more semantically aligned with their formal knowledge). Our results have novel implications for platform design and operations to motivate users to contribute valuable content.

title: EXPRESS: Mind the Cost of Disturbance: Firm-Level Supply Chain Risk and the Bank Loan Cost
authors: Daxuan Cheng; Lei Gao; Yin Liao; Zheyao Pan
abstract: This study investigates whether and how supply chain risk, a core operational vulnerability, is priced in financial credit markets. Using a novel text-based firm-level measure, we show that elevated supply chain risk leads to higher loan interest spreads. Exploiting natural disasters as exogenous shocks to production networks, we provide causal evidence that shocks increase perceived supply chain fragility and, in turn, raise borrowing costs. These effects are amplified when lenders face greater private-information deficiency, and are further strengthened when external information production is more intensive — the former heightening lenders’ concern over supply chain exposure, the latter enhancing their capacity to recognize and price it. Critically, lenders treat supply chain fragility as a form of credit risk: firms with higher supply chain risk face increased default risk, and firms whose production networks are struck by supplier disasters face a higher probability of covenant violation and tighter covenant restrictions, signaling lenders’ anticipation of repayment difficulties. Our findings highlight a new financial consequence of operational risk, showing that supply chain disruption directly affects corporate financing outcomes.

title: EXPRESS: From Institutional Expansion to Exposure-Driven Co-Evolution: Reinterpreting “Operations and Supply Chain Management in China”
authors: Yinghao Pan; Dingyi Tang; Jie Wu; Yuan Sun; Liangfei Qiu
abstract: This paper builds on and reinterprets Wu (2026a,b), which offers a comprehensive account of the rapid institutional, educational, and research development of Operations and Supply Chain Management (OSCM) in China. While the Institutional–Dynamic–Organizational (IDO) framework effectively captures domestic structural transformation, it under-theorizes a critical external driver of this evolution: international knowledge exposure and collaboration. To address this gap, we complement Wu’s analysis with a bibliometric study of published articles in Production and Operations Management from 1992 to 2026. The evidence shows that China’s growing presence in OSCM research is overwhelmingly collaboration-mediated, with China–U.S. co-authorship constituting the dominant channel of integration. The rise of China in top-tier OSCM journals is therefore not primarily an autonomous national trajectory, but a structurally embedded phenomenon within global co-authorship networks. Our findings suggest that China’s OSCM evolution cannot be fully explained by domestic institutional expansion, policy support, or educational scaling alone. Instead, it reflects a broader process of exposure-driven co-evolution within a globally integrated knowledge system. In this system, international collaboration is not merely a byproduct of scientific development but a central mechanism shaping the structure and trajectory of global OSCM knowledge production.

title: Inter-organisational Capabilities and the Transformation of Trust in Blockchain-based Smart Contracts: A Framework for SME Ecosystems
authors: Maksym Koghut; Cathy Urquhart; Soo Hee Lee; Omar Al-Tabbaa
affiliations: University of Kent; Manchester Metropolitan University - All Saints Campus; University of Leeds
abstract: Blockchain-based smart contracts embed agreement enforcement within executable code, constraining the partner discretion that inter-organisational relationships (IORs) have traditionally coordinated through trust, communication, and relational governance. This raises a question that popular accounts tend to foreclose: whether automated enforcement makes inter-organisational trust unnecessary, or whether trust instead changes in function and object. Drawing on expert consultation with 28 blockchain specialists and 25 in-depth interviews with executives, we conduct an inductive study of how IORs transform as organisations adopt smart contracts. We develop a framework in which intensive relational exchange enables organisations to build two inter-organisational capabilities, Distributed Transparency Capability and Algorithmic Coordination Capability, through which they actualise the affordances that smart contracts offer. Through this capability development a distinctive inter-organisational trust form emerges, System-based Trust, defined as warranted reliance on coordinating infrastructure that partner organisations jointly construct. System-based Trust complements rather than replaces relational trust: it carries operational coordination and frees relational trust for strategic collaboration and exception handling, producing Hybrid Inter-organisational Relationships as the outcome of successful transformation. The framework applies to small and medium-sized enterprise ecosystems with limited numbers of trading partners; larger-scale consortia and power-asymmetric networks fall outside its scope. Our findings reposition smart contracts as occasions for capability development rather than substitutes for inter-organisational trust.

title:
<scp>CEO</scp>
                    Ideologically (In)Congruent Activism and Investor Reactions: An Attribution of
                    <scp>CEO</scp>
                    Intentions Perspective
authors: Miao Yun; Longwang Fu
affiliations: City University of Hong Kong; Shanghai Jiao Tong University
abstract: Abstract The phenomenon of chief executive officers (CEOs) taking activism stances on contested sociopolitical issues is increasing, yet it remains unclear how observing investors discern CEO intentions behind activism engagements, thereby shaping their judgments and subsequent reactions. By relaxing the assumption that CEO activism is an unabashed expression of personal beliefs, we propose the concept of CEO ideologically (in)congruent activism and develop a framework wherein investors may attribute CEO intentions underlying incongruent (versus congruent) activism engagements as more organization‐driven (versus self‐driven) interest pursuits, thereby leading to more positive investor evaluations and reactions. Furthermore, we argue that the positive effect of CEO ideologically incongruent activism on investor reactions will be amplified when the CEO owns a higher level of stock ownership but weakened when the firm receives a greater corporate social responsibility (CSR) rating. We corroborate our propositions using a sample of CEO activism events for S&P 500 firms from 2012 to 2021. Our findings demonstrate the heterogeneity and critical influence of CEO intentions behind activism engagements and shed light on how investors integrate multi‐informational cues when evaluating and reacting to managerial incongruent behaviours.

title: Designing Liminal Spaces for Upstream Performativity: Lessons From The Futures Lab
authors: Annmarie Ryan
affiliations: Kemmy Business School, University of Limerick Limerick Ireland
abstract: Abstract This paper examines how business schools can function as liminal socio‐material infrastructures for upstream performative experimentation. Recent work has advanced management scholarship to foreground the role of imagination in theorizing for desirable futures. However, less is understood about how alternatives might be made sufficiently tangible and credible to acquire performative force in the first place. This is compounded by performativity research that has largely examined how theories acquire effects once they circulate in markets and organizations. To address this, and drawing on a 5‐year qualitative case study of The Futures Lab (TFL), I show how shared visual workspaces, repeated critique, direct engagement with stakeholders, and the making and remaking of maps, models and prototypes enabled participants to (re)‐search alternative futures by making possibilities visible, contestable and open to revision. These practices produced credible fictions: tangible yet provisional representations to which external actors could attach, align with, and sometimes enrol around emerging possibilities. I develop prefigurative theorizing as a materially experimental mode of prospective theorizing, showing how desirable futures gain performative force not through imagination alone, but by being externalized, provisionally enacted, tested and revised in the present. The study thereby specifies conditions through which business schools can cultivate upstream performativity.

title: Debt Aversion: Theory and Measurement
authors: David Albrecht; Thomas Meissner
affiliations: WZB Berlin Social Science Center Berlin Germany; Maastricht University Maastricht the Netherlands
abstract: ABSTRACT We propose a model of debt aversion and conduct an experiment with real debt and saving contracts to jointly elicit debt aversion and preferences over time, risk, and intertemporal losses. We find that 89% of participants are debt averse, which strongly influences their choices. The estimated “borrowing premium,” the compensation an average person requires to accept debt, is around 16% of the principal. Applying a validated survey module to a representative sample of German households, we find that debt aversion is both statistically and economically significantly associated with actual debt‐taking and financial health.

title: ON THE RELATION BETWEEN DISCRETE- AND CONTINUOUS-TIME AFFINE OPTION PRICING MODELS
authors: Maciej Augustyniak; Alexandru Badescu; Jean-François Bėgin; Sarath Kumar Jayaraman
affiliations: University of Montreal; University of Calgary; Simon Fraser University
abstract: This article studies the weak convergence of discrete-time generalized autoregressive conditional heteroskedasticity (GARCH) and stochastic volatility (SV) option pricing models that allow for fat tails, multi-component volatilities, and non-monotonic pricing kernels. We introduce a general affine framework that enables the simultaneous derivation of new diffusion limits for Gaussian and inverse Gaussian GARCH models based on distributional invariant parametric convergence rates. When restricted to one-component specifications, our limits yield non-degenerate bivariate diffusions, generalizing the existing results in the affine GARCH literature. By using alternative parametric convergence rates, we further provide a comprehensive classification of all possible limits for two classes of affine and non-affine discrete-time SV models. Specifically, we show that the canonical affine classes of models popularized in discrete and continuous time are not analogous to one another. Our theoretical results are supported by a series of numerical experiments that investigate the impact of parametric scaling assumptions and model features on the convergence of European option prices. Overall, we find that the new limiting diffusions produce option prices that are closest to their discrete-time counterparts sampled at daily frequency.

title: ESTIMATION AND INFERENCE OF NONLINEAR AUTOREGRESSIVE DISTRIBUTED LAG MODELS WITH TIME TREND BY ORDINARY LEAST SQUARES
authors: Jin Seo Cho
affiliations: Yonsei University
abstract: This study examines the large-sample behavior of an ordinary least squares (OLS) estimator within a correctly specified nonlinear autoregressive distributed lag (NARDL) model for nonstationary data. Although the OLS estimator suffers from an asymptotically singular matrix problem, it remains consistent for unknown model parameters and asymptotically follows a mixed normal distribution. Additionally, we examine the large-sample behavior of the standard Wald test, as defined by the OLS estimator, for asymmetries in long- and short-run NARDL parameters, and enhance this analysis with a super-consistent long-run parameter estimator. We then confirm the theory on the Wald test using Monte Carlo simulations. Finally, using U.S. GDP and exogenous fiscal shock data, we demonstrate the use of the OLS estimator and show statistical evidence of long- and short-run symmetries between the effects of tax increases and decreases on U.S. GDP.

title: JACKKNIFE EMPIRICAL LIKELIHOOD FOR INFINITE-ORDER U -STATISTICS
authors: Qing Wang; Yichuan Zhao; Ting Zhang
affiliations: Wellesley College; Georgia State University; University of Georgia
abstract: Infinite-order U -statistics play a vital role in modern statistics. However, given their degree k n $k_n$ k Subscript n depends on the sample size n , quantifying their variability is quite challenging, as fixed-degree theories cannot be directly adopted. In this article, we propose a jackknife empirical likelihood (EL) framework that can be used to construct confidence intervals for an infinite-order U -statistic. We establish sufficient conditions for the limiting chi-squared distribution of the JEL ratio statistic and introduce an efficient partition-sampling realization for practical implementation. To evaluate the performance of the proposed methodology, we conduct simulation studies in the context of subsampling-based ensemble methods and the maximum test, respectively, comparing its performance with four competing methods. The simulation studies yield satisfactory results across the board. Finally, we demonstrate the practical application of our method using a United States Forest Service timber auctions dataset to predict the highest bid at an auction.

title: Correction: Will patents with more interdisciplinary scientific knowledge have higher technological impact? Empirical evidence from USPTO patents
authors: Yuan Xu; Xi Chen; Jin Mao; Gang Li

title: When Acknowledgements Don’t Match: Evidence from Horizon 2020
authors: Matthias Müller
abstract: Abstract Funding acknowledgements have become a valuable data source in recent years. The validity of acknowledgements as indicators of direct project-level support, however, remains contested for several reasons. This study examines the reliability of funding acknowledgement data by comparing publications that acknowledge the European Union’s Horizon 2020 Framework Programme in Scopus with publications officially recorded as project outputs in the CORDIS database. Focusing on social science–related fields, this study conducts aggregate-, project-, and semantic-level analyses to assess the correspondence between acknowledged and administratively recorded funding. The results show a substantial and persistent mismatch: only about half of the publications acknowledging Horizon 2020 funding in Scopus can be linked to a corresponding project in CORDIS. This divergence is persistent over time, occurs across funding instruments and subject areas, and is unlikely to be explained solely by reporting delays, administrative incompleteness, or technical matching limitations alone. Instead, the semantic analysis indicates that many unmatched publications are thematically more distant from the confirmed research core of funded projects, suggesting that funding acknowledgements in bibliographic metadata capture also broader, indirect, or non-project-core relations to funding beyond formally reported project outputs.

title: Measuring research-related academic performance in a comprehensive university: individual heterogeneity, institutional context, and multidimensional output profiles
authors: Claudiu Vasile Kifor; Horațiu Rusu; Ana-Maria Benedek; Ioan Sîrbu; Roxana Florența Săvescu
abstract: Abstract Assessing research-related academic performance remains a central challenge in scientometrics because scholarly output is multidimensional, unevenly distributed across individuals, and embedded in disciplinary and institutional contexts. This study examines the relative contribution of between-individual heterogeneity and institutional context to research-related academic performance in a Romanian comprehensive public university, using a five-year panel dataset comprising 444 academic staff members and 2,220 person-year observations from 2017 to 2021. Performance was measured through two complementary approaches: a relative performance indicator expressing each individual’s annual research score in relation to the benchmark for their current academic position, and a multidimensional activity profile based on 20 research-output indicators. Generalized linear mixed models, exploratory generalized additive models (GAM), and multivariate constrained ordination were used. The most parsimonious mixed model retained year, age, academic title, and study field and yielded a marginal R 2 of 23% and a conditional R 2 of 78%. Constrained ordination showed a similar pattern, with respondent identity explaining 49.79% of adjusted variation in activity profiles. Over time, output profiles shifted toward Q1/Q2 publications and independent citations. In the GAM analysis, work seniority was not associated with relative performance, whereas time since last promotion showed a nonlinear relationship, with performance increasing during the first years after promotion and declining thereafter. Overall, persistent between-individual differences accounted for the largest share of structured variation, while institutional, field-specific, and career-stage factors contributed to differences in the level and composition of academic output.

title: Citation accuracy, citation noise, and citation bias: a foundation of citation analysis
authors: Lutz Bornmann; Christian Leibel
abstract: Abstract Citation analysis is widely used in research evaluation to assess the impact of scientific papers. These analyses rest on the assumption that citation decisions by authors are accurate, representing the flow of knowledge from cited to citing papers. However, in practice, researchers often cite for reasons that are not related to the fact that there has been (intellectual) input from previous papers. Citations made for rhetorical reasons or without reading the cited work compromise the value of citations as instrument for research evaluation. Past research on threats to the accuracy of citations has mainly focused on citation bias as the primary concern. In this paper, we argue that citation noise—the undesirable variance in citation decisions—represents an equally critical but underexplored challenge in citation analysis. We define and differentiate two types of citation noise: citation level noise and citation pattern noise. Each type of noise is described in terms of how it arises and the specific ways it can undermine the validity of citation-based research assessments. By conceptually differing citation noise from citation accuracy and citation bias, we propose a framework for the foundation of citation analysis. We discuss strategies and interventions to minimize citation noise, aiming to improve the reliability and validity of citation analysis in research evaluation. We recommend that the current professional reform movement in research evaluation such as the Coalition for Advancing Research Assessment (CoARA) pick up these strategies and interventions as an additional building block for careful, responsible use of bibliometric indicators in research evaluation.

title: Measuring Measurement Error
authors: N Aaron Pancost; Garrett Schaller
affiliations: University of Texas at Austin , McCombs School of Business; Colorado State University , College of Business
abstract: Abstract We collect 2,848 instrumental variable (IV) regressions from 391 papers published in top economics and finance journals and show that estimated IV coefficients are often much larger than their OLS counterparts, even when theory suggests they should be smaller. We derive meta-regression estimators that distinguish measurement error bias from omitted variable bias and simultaneity bias; applying our estimators to a set of 1,040 comparable regressions from 139 papers, we find that measurement error shrinks reported coefficients by about two to four times. Measurement error remains quantitatively important even after accounting for weak instruments, publication bias, instrument invalidity, and heterogeneous treatment effects. Our results suggest that measurement error is a severe, pervasive, and understated source of bias in economics and finance.

title: Talent Attraction Policies, Corporate Innovation, and Spillover Effects
authors: Thomas J Chemmanur; Di Tang; Chaopeng Wu

title: Environmental Incidents and Sustainability Pricing Provisions
authors: HUYEN NGUYEN; SOCHIMA UZONWANNE
abstract: Abstract We investigate whether lenders use sustainability pricing provisions (SPPs) to manage borrower environmental risk. Using unexpected negative environmental incidents as shocks to environmental risk, we find that lenders are 10 percentage points less likely to include SPPs in loans to environmentally risky borrowers. Instead, they rely on conventional tools, including higher interest rates, stricter covenants, and collateral requirements. The effect weakens under strong institutional investor demand or when lenders can sell loans in secondary markets. Our study suggests that SPPs primarily help attract institutional investors rather than manage risk, with implications for the design and regulation of sustainability‐linked financial instruments.

title: Beyond Greenwashing: Environmental Commitments and Gas Flaring in the African Oil Sector
authors: Samuel Chang; Hans B. Christensen; Andrew McKinley
affiliations: The University of Chicago; Northwestern University
abstract: ABSTRACT Corporations make substantial progress toward their Zero Routine Flaring commitments globally, particularly in Africa where preexisting environmental standards are weak. Moreover, committers’ flaring reductions on the continent are driven primarily by operational improvements rather than offloading assets and are concentrated among committers facing greater stakeholder pressure. Although flaring is higher for assets continuously operated by, awarded to, or divested to noncommitters, corporate actions to uphold commitments are associated with a conservatively estimated 10 percent net reduction in flaring in Africa without a corresponding reduction in oil production or local economic activity in extraction communities. Our findings suggest that environmental commitments are backed by corporate policies akin to establishing a uniform cost of pollution across the firm’s global operations and therefore may alleviate the problems posed by globally fragmented regulation.
